learning_objective: 🎯 Understand the invisible water floating all around us! Learn how it turns into clouds, dew, fog, and eventually falls back to Earth as rain or snow.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Humidity is the amount of invisible water vapour in the air. 'Absolute Humidity' is the actual weight of water in a volume of air. 'Relative Humidity' is a percentage showing how full the air is compared to its maximum capacity at that temperature.

When warm, moist air cools down, it can't hold as much water. The invisible vapour turns back into liquid drops. If this happens near the ground, we get Dew, Frost, or Fog. If it happens high in the sky, we get Clouds.
Clouds are classified by height and shape: Cirrus (high, feathery ice clouds), Cumulus (puffy, cotton-like clouds), Stratus (low, flat, grey blanket clouds), and Nimbus (dark rain clouds).

Rain happens in three main ways: Convectional (hot air rises, cools, and rains quickly), Orographic (wind is forced up over a mountain, cooling and raining on one side), and Cyclonic/Frontal (warm air is pushed up by a heavy cold air mass).

fun_activity.title: 🧊 The Sweating Glass
fun_activity.instructions: Fill a glass with ice water and place it on a table on a warm day. In a few minutes, the outside of the glass will be completely wet. The glass isn't leaking! The cold glass cooled the warm air around it, causing the invisible water vapour in the air to 'condense' into liquid drops.

exam_tips: 📌 Relative Humidity is highly dependent on temperature. If you heat the air, its capacity to hold water increases, so its Relative Humidity decreases.
📌 The 'Dew Point' is the exact temperature at which the air becomes 100% saturated and condensation begins.
📌 In Orographic rainfall, the 'Windward' side of the mountain gets heavy rain, while the 'Leeward' side (Rain Shadow Area) remains dry.
quick_recap: ⭐ Water exists in the atmosphere in three forms: solid (snow/ice), liquid (rain/water), and gas (vapour).
⭐ Condensation requires tiny dust or smoke particles (condensation nuclei) for water to grab onto.
⭐ Nimbus clouds are the ones that bring continuous rain or thunderstorms.
